planting.note: Plant container shrubs after frost danger passes in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; this is the wild, unselected Chinese species behind virtually every butterfly bush cultivar on the market.

directions: Buddleja davidii is the wild species collected in central China in the 1890s and named for the missionary-naturalist Armand David, and it is the parent of nearly all the named butterfly bush cultivars sold today, from Black Knight to the dwarf Pugster and Lo and Behold series. Left unselected, it grows into a large, loose, fountain-shaped shrub with gray-green lance-shaped leaves and long, arching, honey-scented lilac-purple flower spikes that draw butterflies, bees, and hummingbirds from summer into fall. It flowers on new wood, so cut the entire plant back hard to 12-18 inches each late winter to keep it full and floriferous rather than tall and leggy. Because the species sets abundant viable seed, it has naturalized and is considered invasive in parts of the Pacific Northwest and mid-Atlantic; deadhead spent spikes before they set seed where this is a concern, or choose one of the sterile modern cultivars instead.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, siting with afternoon shade in hot-summer climates; this is the wild green-leaved species from which nearly all red, purple, lace-leaf, and dwarf Japanese maple cultivars were selected.

directions: Acer palmatum is the straight species native to the woodlands of Japan, Korea, and China, growing as a small, often multi-trunked understory tree with fresh green, palmately five- to seven-lobed leaves that turn gold, orange, or crimson in fall. It is considerably larger and faster-growing than the named dwarf or weeping selections bred from it, and its seedlings show more natural variation in leaf shape and fall color than named clones. Give it consistent moisture and protection from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind, especially in zones 7-8, where leaf scorch is the most common problem; a site with dappled shade and shelter from exposed, windy locations mimics its native woodland-edge habitat best. Prune only to remove dead, crossing, or awkward branches in winter dormancy, since heavy pruning in leaf disrupts its naturally graceful, layered branching habit.
sources: Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this full-size species, not the many dwarf globe and pyramidal cultivars bred from it, is the native northeastern conifer also called eastern white cedar.

directions: Thuja occidentalis is the wild North American conifer of cool northern forests, limestone cliffs, and swamp edges, growing as a narrow pyramidal tree with soft, flattened sprays of aromatic, scale-like foliage and shredding reddish-brown bark, far larger over time than the compact globe and dwarf cultivars sold for foundation plantings. It tolerates wet, swampy soils and alkaline limestone sites better than most conifers, and it is one of the most reliably winter-hardy evergreens for cold northern gardens, but mature plantings are a favored winter browse of white-tailed deer, which can disfigure young trees badly where deer pressure is high. Grow it as a specimen, windbreak, or screening hedge rather than a foundation plant given its eventual size, and avoid heavy shearing of a mature leader, since old wood on arborvitae does not reliably resprout if cut back hard. It needs little fertilizing once established and is remarkably long-lived, with wild trees documented at well over 500 years old on rocky Canadian Shield outcrops.
sources: Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this green-leaved wild species, not the purple-leaved or dwarf cultivars bred from it, is restricted or banned from sale in several northeastern and midwestern states for its invasive spread into woodlands.

directions: Berberis thunbergii is the wild Japanese shrub behind the many purple-, gold-, and variegated-leaved barberry cultivars common in American gardens, forming a dense, thorny, mounded shrub with small green leaves, pale yellow spring flowers, and bright red berries that persist into winter and color the fall foliage orange-red. It is extremely tolerant of poor, dry, or compacted soil, road salt, and urban pollution, which once made it a go-to hedging and foundation shrub, but its berries are spread widely by birds and the species has become seriously invasive in woodlands and old fields across the Northeast and Upper Midwest, leading several states to restrict or ban its sale. Where it remains legal and appropriate to plant, give it full sun for the densest growth and best berry and fall color display, and prune after flowering if a tidier shape is wanted, since its thorny branches make hand-pruning as a hedge painful work. Gardeners in regions where the species is restricted should choose a native alternative, such as inkberry or winterberry, rather than seeking out the straight species.
sources: USDA Forest Service Invasive Species Database
Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; this East Asian species, smaller-leaved and generally hardier than common English boxwood, is the parent of Winter Gem, Green Pillow, and most other Japanese boxwood cultivars.

directions: Buxus microphylla is the small-leaved boxwood species native to Japan and Korea, forming a dense, rounded, slow-growing evergreen with fine-textured foliage that is generally more cold-hardy and heat-tolerant than the larger-leaved common boxwood, Buxus sempervirens. Its foliage often takes on a bronze or yellowish winter cast in cold climates, a trait bred out of many modern cultivars but typical of the straight species. Give it well-drained soil amended with organic matter and consistent moisture, since shallow boxwood roots dry out quickly, and avoid piling mulch against the stems, which encourages the root and stem fungal diseases that trouble the genus. Light shearing in late spring maintains a formal shape, while unclipped plants develop a softer, naturally rounded form well suited to informal hedges or foundation plantings.
sources: Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

planting.note: Blooms on old wood in spring; prune lightly right after flowering only to shape (Group 1), since hard pruning removes next year's flowering wood. This wild Asian species is the parent of named macropetala cultivars such as Markham's Pink and White Swan.

directions: Clematis macropetala is a wild species native to northern China, Mongolia, and Siberia, bearing nodding, bell-shaped, violet-blue flowers in mid spring whose inner petaloid staminodes give each bloom a soft, double-looking fluffiness distinct from the single, flat-faced flowers of large-hybrid clematis groups. It flowers earliest of any clematis in the garden, often before the vine has even fully leafed out, and the silvery, feathery seed heads that follow extend its ornamental interest well into summer. Because it blooms entirely on the previous year's wood, prune only lightly right after flowering to remove dead growth and control size; a hard winter or spring cutback, appropriate for large summer-blooming hybrids, will sacrifice the entire spring flower display. Extremely cold hardy and easy to grow on a mailbox post, low fence, or large shrub to scramble through, it needs only average garden soil and consistent moisture to establish.

planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions after frost danger passes in well-drained soil in full sun; this green-leaved wild species, the parent of the far more common purple-leaved 'Rubrum' cultivar, is a true perennial only in zones 9-10 and is grown as a warm-season annual elsewhere.

directions: Pennisetum setaceum is the wild, green-foliaged form of fountain grass native to East Africa and the Middle East, forming an arching, fine-textured clump topped from summer through fall with soft, bristly, pinkish-tan plumes that nod gracefully in the slightest breeze. Unlike the widely sold, sterile, purple-leaved 'Rubrum' cultivar bred from it, the straight species sets abundant viable seed and has become seriously invasive in frost-free climates such as Hawaii, southern California, and Arizona, so gardeners in zones 9-10 should deadhead spent plumes before they shatter or choose 'Rubrum' instead. Where winters kill it back, treat it as a fast, easy warm-season annual grown from a nursery plug after the last frost. It thrives in full sun and lean, well-drained soil with minimal supplemental water once established, and tolerates heat, salt spray, and drought far better than most ornamental grasses.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this Chinese species, not the European plum, is the parent of most American and Japanese dessert plum cultivars such as Santa Rosa, Methley, and Shiro, and most selections need a compatible cross-pollinizer.

directions: Prunus salicina is native to China, despite the common name Japanese plum, and reached the West via Japan in the 19th century; it is the species behind the great majority of dessert plum cultivars grown in home orchards today, prized for juicy, sweet, richly flavored fruit that ripens over a longer summer window than European plums. It blooms earlier in spring than European plum, which makes it more vulnerable to late frost damage in marginal climates, and most cultivars are self-incompatible, requiring a second compatible variety blooming at the same time for fruit set. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil, and prune to an open center form each winter to admit light and air into the canopy, which improves fruit size and reduces brown rot in humid climates. Thin heavily set fruit to four to six inches apart along the branch in late spring to prevent limb breakage and to concentrate size and sugar into the remaining plums.
sources: University of California Fruit & Nut Research Center

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early to mid fall in deep, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial afternoon shade; this wild Chinese tree peony species, distinct from the more common garden hybrid Paeonia suffruticosa, is the source of the Gansu Mudan group of Chinese tree peonies.

directions: Paeonia rockii is a wild tree peony species restricted to limestone mountain forests of Gansu and Shaanxi provinces in northwest China, named for the plant explorer Joseph Rock, who collected and introduced it to Western cultivation in the mid-20th century. It bears large, single to semi-double white or pale pink flowers marked at the base of each petal with a distinctive dark maroon-purple blotch, a flower pattern quite different from the typically unmarked, fully double blooms of the more familiar Chinese and Japanese tree peony hybrids. Slow-growing and long-lived, it forms a woody, multi-stemmed shrub that resents disturbance once established, so choose a permanent site with deep, fertile, well-drained soil and some afternoon shade in hot summer climates. Set the graft union, if present, below the soil surface to encourage the scion to develop its own root system, and avoid heavy pruning, since flowers form on growth from the previous season.
